\title{Collective Defined Contribution Schemes Without Intergenerational Cross-Subsidies}
\author{\small{John Armstrong\textsuperscript{a}, James Dalby\textsuperscript{b}, Rohan Hobbs\textsuperscript{c}}\\
\small{\textsuperscript{a,b,c}Department of Mathematics, King's College London, UK}\\
\small{\textsuperscript{a,*}john.armstrong@kcl.ac.uk, \textsuperscript{b}james.dalby@kcl.ac.uk, \textsuperscript{c}rohan.hobbs@kcl.ac.uk} }
\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
    We present an architecture for managing Collective Defined Contribution (CDC) schemes. The current approach to UK CDC can be described as shared-indexation, where the nominal benefit of every member in a scheme receives the same level of indexation each year. The design of such schemes rely on the use of approximate discounting methodologies to value liabilities, and this leads to intergenerational cross-subsidies which can be large and unpredictable.
    We present an alternative approach which we call {\em Collective-Drawdown CDC}. This approach does not
    result in intergenerational cross-subsidies
    since all pooling is performed by explicit insurance contracts. It is therefore completely fair. Moreover, this scheme results in better pension outcomes when compared to shared-indexation CDC under the same model parameters.
\end{abstract}


\section{Introduction}


Collective Defined Contribution (CDC) pension schemes have now arrived in the UK following the opening of the Royal Mail Collective Pension Plan (RMCPP) \cite{royalMailTrustDeeds, royalMailHandbook}. In the current framework of UK CDC, contribution rates
are fixed as a percentage of salaries, benefits paid out vary and risks are shared collectively \cite{cdcRegulations}. The main risks proposed to be shared are investment and longevity risk for the purpose of delivering better outcomes in retirement.

The RMCPP is a {\em shared-indexation} CDC scheme with {\em flat accrual}.
In a shared-indexation CDC scheme, all members receive a certain level of {\em nominal benefit} each year in exchange for their contributions. In the RMCPP, the nominal benefit obtained for a given level of contribution is fixed, irrespective of age, which is why we call it a flat-accrual scheme. Each year, a level of indexation is chosen to ensure assets match liabilities and then this level is applied uniformly to all members' accrued nominal benefit entitlements. Because the accrual rate is the same for all ages in the RMCPP, this leads to significant intergenerational cross-subsidies. An alternative approach to a shared-indexation CDC scheme is a {\em dynamic-accrual} scheme, where the nominal benefit received for a given level of contribution takes into account the time-value of investments. Modelling and simulations of such schemes can be found in \cite{upton, armstrong_dalby_donnelly}.

The flat-accrual approach results
in large cross subsidies between
generations, with the benefit entitlements of older generations being worth far more than that of younger generations in exchange for the same contribution. This is reduced significantly in the dynamic-accrual approach.
However, dynamic-accrual schemes do not perfectly value nominal benefits due to the use of an approximate discounting methodology. As a result, there remain significant cross-subsidies in these schemes and they are stochastic (see \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly} for a detailed study of cross subsidy).


In this paper, we study an alternative CDC scheme design that delivers the proposed benefits of CDC without any cross-subsidies, whilst also outperforming shared-indexation CDC. We call the scheme \emph{Collective-Drawdown} CDC. This is because each member has a known fund value, as in a Defined-Contribution (DC) scheme, but members are additionally insured against longevity risk via an internal insurance market. This approach will, by design, not contain any cross-subsidies. We still consider our approach to be a form of CDC because it pools longevity risk collectively rather than relying on an external insurer or an employer covenant, and operates on a defined-contribution basis. Some readers may take a different view on what are the defining features of a ``CDC scheme'', but we believe that from the points-of-view of both policy makers and scheme members, these are the key features. 

The internal insurance market in individual longevity risk is the defining feature of collective-drawdown. It is a simple extension of a classical tontine mechanism that is completely fair, even for a heterogenous pool of individuals. This is because we separate investment risk and longevity risk when calculating an individuals longevity payment which is weighted according to an individuals expected contribution to the market over a given period. This ensures contributions satisfy actuarial fairness and tontine payments are fair for each individual. This is essential if such a market is to be implemented in practice. 

Other tontine payments for heterogenous funds that satisfy some definition of fairness have been suggested. For example, \cite{milevsky2016} uses a definition of equitable to determine payments. This means each individual loses an identical fraction of their wealth to the tontine i.e., the present value of future payments are all slightly less than the initial contribution. \cite{chen} extends this work by deriving a numerical procedure to achieve approximate fairness, in the sense that payments for policyholders are almost identical among all different cohorts. A very similar approach to ours is given in \cite{donnelly2014}, where the payment received by each member of a group is proportional to their individual wealth and force
of mortality, and this achieves actuarial fairness. The key difference with our approach is that payments are determined on an individual basis, rather than a group/cohort basis, so every member can be different, and we show how this mechanism can operate in discrete time which makes it much simpler to explain to members and allows for investment in illiquid assets. %all heterogeneity can be accounted for and no approximations or definitions are required.

More generally, the simplicity and flexibility of tontines mean that numerous optimal investment problems into innovative pension products utilising them have been studied. Some examples of the rich set of schemes tontines can facilitate include, tontines with minimum guaranteed payouts \cite{chenAndRach}, pooled annuity funds \cite{stamos, donnelly2014}, combinations of annuities and tontines \cite{chenRachSehner2020, milevsky2015}, as well as splitting funds between an individual/bequest account and a tontine account subject to different rules \cite{boadoPenas, donelly_bernhardt}. A review of the long history of tontines and the more recent literature can be found in \cite{milevsky}. Thus while our term ``collective drawdown'' is new, the idea of pension vehicle that combines an investment strategy chosen by an adviser or algorithm with a tontine is not. We nevertheless think that it is helpful to provide a label for such a vehicle.

This longevity risk market could also be of benefit within classical CDC schemes to maximize the pooling of longevity risk. For this reason, we begin by proposing an overall architecture which can be used by a pension provider to efficiently manage multiple schemes, which might include both collective-drawdown schemes and shared-indexation schemes.

We compare the performance of shared-indexation and collective-drawdown approaches in a Black--Scholes model. Since shared-indexation CDC
has a design that does not incorporate any detailed beliefs about the market, a simple model such as the Black--Scholes model seems a fairer test of their relative performance than a more complex model, as a collective-drawdown scheme could be tuned to match these complexities. The optimal investment strategy used for the collective-drawdown fund is found using a neural network, rather than solving a classical HJB equation directly. We expect that this approach would continue to work well in more complex market models. 

Our key finding is that the collective-drawdown approach is better able to produce an ``income for life'' than shared-indexation schemes.
The collective-drawdown approach also achieves this without any intergenerational cross-subsidies. We demonstrate this numerically by finding a strategy that most would agree out-performs shared-indexation CDC. We also show that in complete markets, collective drawdown is optimal in the sense that under very mild assumptions on preferences, there are no mutually beneficial schemes that can improve upon collective drawdown.

We also argue that the collective-drawdown approach is simpler to interpret than shared-indexation schemes. This may seem counter-intuitive since we use a neural network to compute the optimal strategy for our collective-drawdown approach. However, we argue that the closed-form formula used in shared-indexation CDC is not as simple to interpret as it may seem: a shared-indexation CDC contract is a path-dependent derivative whose behaviour also depends upon the future demographic profile of the scheme. 

The paper is organised as follows. In \Cref{sec:architecture}, we describe the proposed architecture. In particular, we describe how an internal longevity insurance market could operate and how multiple employers can be combined. In \Cref{sec:CDCpooling}, we describe how we model a shared-indexation scheme. In \Cref{sec:insuredDrawdown}, we describe how we model a collective-drawdown fund and select its optimal investment strategy. In \Cref{sec:results}, we show pension outcomes from a collective-drawdown fund and compare these to a shared-indexation fund subject to the same model parameters. In \Cref{sec:discussion}, we discuss the practical
pros and cons of different approaches. In \Cref{sec:conclusions}, some conclusions are presented.


\section{An architecture for multi-employer CDC}\label{sec:architecture}
\begin{figure}[h!tbp]
    \centering
        \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{Pictures/FundDiagrams.pdf}
    \caption{CDC provider architecture.}
    \label{fig:design}
\end{figure}
The overall architecture we propose for a provider
of  collective defined contribution pensions is shown in Figure
\ref{fig:design}.
Each employee is a member of one scheme that has been set up
to meet the needs of one or more employers. The members themselves
are not expected to make complex decisions about pension investments.
Instead, they simply choose what contributions to make (with sensible default levels already chosen for them) and, ultimately, receive the benefits from the scheme. This is the {\em member layer} of the design.

The {\em employer layer} is where strategic decision making takes place.
This determines the types of scheme which should be available to
the employees, the rules by which these schemes operate, and
the investment and benefit targets the schemes will achieve. It
is efficient to make these decisions at the employer level. Strategic
decision making requires too much financial expertise for most
members to be able to engage with this process.  However, by providing
customization at the employer level, the differing needs
of different types of employee can be catered for.

A central feature of a CDC scheme is that it should perform
longevity pooling. This requires some form of underwriting. Underwriting should be performed at the level of strategic decision making to ensure that all parties who decide upon an insurance contract have access to the same information. It will normally be much cheaper to perform underwriting for an employer as a whole rather than for each individual member. There will be much less opportunity for manipulation of private information about one's health if longevity insurance is agreed at the employer layer, rather than the member layer. Thus, we propose that the internal insurance market operates at the employer level. We also propose that longevity insurance operates between employers, not just within individual schemes. This will maximize the potential benefits of longevity pooling.

Finally, in the {\em investment layer}, the provider must make concrete, tactical investment
decisions to meet the strategic goals of each scheme. The expertise
needed to make these decisions can be pooled across all employers,
and investment decisions can be netted to reduce costs. To achieve this, the provider can create an investment layer containing a small number of managed portfolios such as a growth portfolio invested in equities and a low-risk portfolio invested in index-linked gilts.
The strategic decision making at the employer layer is translated into
a decision about how to weight investments across these portfolios.
The job of the investment layer is the day-to-day management of
these shared portfolios.

This design is intended to minimize costs, which are indicated in italics in Figure \ref{fig:design}. Underwriting costs occur at the employer layer. Transaction costs occur at the investment layer and are reduced by netting. The
provider can use the same fundamental scheme design for multiple employers which should result in reduced costs for scheme approval.

\subsection{The internal insurance market}

Let us suppose that there are a finite number of schemes combined within the provider. Write $\cal{S}$ for the set of schemes. Each year, each scheme, $\alpha \in {\cal S}$, has $n_\alpha$ members whose probability of surviving over the period is $p^i_\alpha$ ($1 \leq i \leq n_\alpha)$. We label each member with the pair $(\alpha,i)$. Associated with each individual is an investment strategy $q^i_\alpha$, determining the quantity invested in the different portfolios. The total value of these portfolios should equal the total value of the scheme.

At the end of each year, the market value of each individual's fund will be $v^i_\alpha$. Let $D^i_\alpha$ be an indicator taking the
value $1$ if individual $i$ in fund $\alpha$ dies over the period. The total
funds available to the longevity pool will then be given
\[
F = \sum_{\alpha \in {\cal S}} \sum_{j=1}^{n_\alpha} D^j_\alpha v^j_\alpha.
\]
These funds are then shared among survivors in proportion to
their expected contribution once $v^i_\alpha$ is known. So,
the amount received by individual $(\alpha,i)$ will be
\begin{equation}
\frac{F (1-D^i_\alpha) (1-p^i_\alpha) v^i_\alpha}{\sum_{\alpha\in {\cal S}} \sum_{j=1}^{n_\alpha}(1-D^j_\alpha)(1- p^j_\alpha) v^j_\alpha}.
\label{eq:longevityCredit}
\end{equation}

This differs slightly from a classical survivor fund design,
because each individual is investing different quantities in each portfolio. As the
pooling of assets occurs using the fund value at the end of the period, investors are shielded from the investment decisions of other
members and the pooling is based only on longevity risk. This simple
device enables longevity pooling across heterogeneous funds.

We remark that although we envisage the probabilities $p^i_\alpha$ to be determined at the start of the investment period, it would be possible to use probabilities determined at the end of the investment period based on the more accurate mortality information known at that date. For example, one might choose to use national-level mortality in a given year for a given age group, rather than the prediction made of this level in the previous year.

This approach to pricing individual longevity risk is intuitive, but there is some scope
for further improvement. If an atypically wealthy investor joins the pool with a large fund size and a large probability of dying in a given year, this may represent a large risk for typical investors in the longevity pool and so, ideally, longevity insurance should be priced somewhat higher for such atypical investors. One simple approach would be simply to place a cap on the maximum of the product of fund size and probability of dying, and only allow individuals to participate in the longevity market up to this cap. As a variation on this, one could have a number of pools each with a cap which investors use in sequence. Thus, there would be one large shared pool for all investors and then smaller pools used only by high net-worth individuals. As we will see in Section \ref{sec:results}, the simple single-pool design already performs very well in practice. This longevity insurance mechanism is essentially a form of tontine, except that it allows individuals to choose different investments. 


\section{Modelling a shared-indexation scheme}
\label{sec:CDCpooling}

Let us now describe a simple version of a shared-indexation scheme. 
In the long term, flat-accrual schemes give worse outcomes in retirement for a given level of contribution than dynamic-accrual schemes \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly}. Therefore, we will focus our attention on dynamic-accrual schemes as the most effective form of shared-indexation CDC. We now describe what is termed a \emph{standard dynamic-accrual} scheme in \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly}, which models the current understanding of UK multi-employer CDC.

We model a simple scheme which contains $M$ different generations, where all members in each generation
are identical apart from their individual mortality. Let $N^g_t$ denote the number of individuals in generation $g$ ($0\leq g <M$)
alive at time $t \in {\mathbb N}$. Let $p^g(t,\ell)$ be the probability that an individual in generation $g$, who is alive at time $t$, is still alive at time $t+\ell$. Let
${\mathbf 1}^{R,g}_{t}$ be an indicator function taking the value $1$ if members of generation $g$ are receiving a pension at time $t$. The fund invests in a pre-determined
asset mix at each time $t$. We define an associated discount factor $P(t,\ell)$ by:
\[
P(t,\ell)^{-1}=1 + e(t,\ell) ,
\]
where $e(t,\ell)$ are the expected returns of the investment strategy over the period $[t,t+\ell]$. We write $\pi_t$ for the proportion invested in risky assets in year $t$.

In our shared-indexation scheme, each member has a nominal benefit entitlement $B^{g, \cum}$, which is equal to zero when they join the scheme.
Each year a {\em nominal indexation rate}, $h^n_t$, is selected and a level of benefit cuts/bonuses  is determined by a parameter $\theta_t$. The initial choice of $h^n_0$ is made by the scheme designer. The scheme designer also chooses an acceptable range $[h^n_{\min},h^n_{\max}]$ for the level of indexation each year.
The nominal benefit for each member at the start of the next period, before any further
contributions are made, will then be given by the equation
\begin{equation}
B^{g,\cum}_{t-}:= (1 + h^n_t) \theta_t B^{g,\cum}_{t-1} \quad \text{if }t>0.
\label{eq:cdcDefining}
\end{equation}


The values of $h^n_t$ and $\theta_t$ in years $t>0$, are determined by the total asset value at time $t$ before payments in and out of the scheme, which we denote by $A_{t-}$. We then
require that $h^n_t$ and $\theta_t$ satisfy the equation
\begin{equation}
A_{t-} = \theta_t \sum_{g=0}^{M-1} \sum_{\ell=0}^\infty (1+h^n_t)^\ell P(t,\ell) N^g_t B^{g,\cum}_{t-1} p^g(t,\ell) {\mathbf 1}^{R,g}_{t+\ell}.
\label{eq:cdcGrowth}
\end{equation}
If it is possible to solve this equation with $h^n_t \in [h^n_{\min},h^n_{\max}]$ and $\theta_t=1$, then these are the values selected. Otherwise, we take $h^n_t=h^n_{\min}$ or $h^n_t=h^n_{\max}$ and then choose $\theta_t<1$ or $\theta_t>1$ respectively, as to solve this equation. In the latter cases, a benefit cut or bonus is said to have occurred.

Once $h^n_t$ has been determined, the additional benefit entitlement, $B^g_t$, received by generation $g$ in exchange for a contribution, $C^g_t$, satisfies:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:multiemployerBenefit}
C^g_t = B^g_t \sum_{\ell=1}^\infty (1+h^n_t)^\ell P(t,\ell)   p^g(t,\ell) {\mathbf 1}^{R,g}_{t+\ell
}.
\end{equation}
The new cumulative benefit entitlement for each generation is
\[
B^{g,\cum}_t = B^{g,\cum}_{t-}+B^g_t.
\]
The pension received by each generation is equal to
\[
B^{g,\cum}_t {\mathbf 1}^{R,g}_{t}.
\]
The fund asset value after benefit payments and contributions is given by
\begin{equation}
A_{t+} := A_{t-} + \sum_{g=0}^{M-1} N^g_t (C^g_t - B^{g,\cum}_t {\mathbf 1}^{R,g}_t).
\label{eq:increments}
\end{equation}


So far, we have described the standard approach to a shared-indexation scheme
with dynamic-accrual without the benefit of a longevity-insurance market.
If there is a longevity-insurance market, we can attempt to benefit from this by
associating the quantity 
\begin{equation}
\sum_{\ell=1}^\infty (1+h^n_t)^\ell P(t,\ell)  B^{g,\cum}_t p^g(t,\ell) {\mathbf 1}^{R,g}_{t+\ell},
\end{equation}
to each individual in generation $g$ in the fund. If this individual dies, this is the quantity
that will be pooled. The proportion invested in risky assets will be the same for all individuals
and will match the investment strategy of the fund. The funds associated to each individual at the end of the period and after the application of longevity credits can then be pooled together again, to compute the total fund value.

For funds with infinite membership, this would result in an identical result to standard shared-indexation schemes. It would also yield identical results for a provider containing a single shared-indexation scheme. However, one would expect it to yield better results for small shared-indexation schemes within a large provider, due to the sharing of the longevity pool across employers.

Currently, UK legislation on CDC schemes requires different sections to operate independently.
Thus, this proposal represents a modest change to current CDC designs.


\section{Modelling a collective-drawdown scheme}
\label{sec:insuredDrawdown}

We now propose an alternative scheme design to take advantage of the
longevity pooling mechanism.

\subsection{General collective-drawdown schemes}

In a collective-drawdown fund, a separate account is maintained at
all times for each investor $(\alpha,i)$ (recall that $\alpha$ numbers the schemes and $i$ the individual within scheme $\alpha$). An employer may offer a small number of different scheme choices and customizations for their employees, perhaps with different risk profiles, but after this, decisions on investment and consumption each year will be determined at the employer-level. This frees members from the task of 
strategic decision making. 

One simple way to choose an investment
and consumption strategy would be to 
specify a fixed life-styling strategy for investment, and a similar table
indicating what proportion of one's wealth to consume each year in retirement. In the next section, we give a more sophisticated
approach to choosing
an investment and consumption strategy that does not use fixed tables. Instead, we identify an optimal strategy by solving a problem
similar to that of Merton \cite{merton1969lifetime}, but additionally take into account mortality risk, longevity pooling, and use a more realistic utility function.

Our example is intended to be illustrative. There is considerable scope in the
design of collective-drawdown schemes to incorporate a wealth of features. Our
intention is simply to give an example of what is possible.




\subsection{The preference model in our simulations}
\label{sec:loss}

We now describe a concrete optimization problem which we use
to determine the collective-drawdown strategy in this paper. Building on \cite{stamos},
the paper \cite{armstrong_buescu_dalby} examines various tractable optimal
investment strategies which account for individual longevity risk in the Black--Scholes model, but finds that these lead to unreasonable strategies. In that paper, it is
argued that the problem with analytically tractable approaches to optimal investment, can be traced to their use of positively homogeneous preferences such as power utilities or Epstein--Zin preferences. We therefore use an alternative preference model that breaks positive homogeneity, and therefore leads to problems which can only be solved numerically.

To describe our preferences, we assume that at each time $t$ after retirement at time $t_{\RA}$, the individual consumes an amount $c_t$. We define
a function
\[
u(c_t,a)=\frac{c_t^\rho}{\rho}-\frac{a^\rho}{\rho}
\]
where ${\rho}<1$ and $a>0$ are parameters whose interpretation we explain shortly.
We assume that each individual seeks to maximize a utility function of the following form,
\begin{equation*}
    U = \mathbb{E}\left( -\text{exp}\left(-\alpha \sum_{t=t_{\RA}}^{t<\tau} u(c_t,a) \delta t\right)\right).
\end{equation*}
The parameter $\alpha>0$ is a risk aversion parameter. The variable $\tau$ is a random variable denoting the time of death, which is assumed to always be greater than $t_\RA$. The size of a time step is $\delta t=1$, The parameter 
$\rho$ is a satiation parameter i.e., it determines the rate at which the individual becomes satiated due to consumption at a given time. We will call the parameter $a$ 
the {\em adequacy level}, because consumption below the adequacy level in a given year decreases utility.  We have omitted indices to indicate the dependence on the individual for ease of notation.

These preferences are a variation on the concept of Kihlstrom--Mirman preferences \cite{kihlstromMirman},
but additionally incorporate mortality. Kihlstrom--Mirman preferences are not commonly used
in general economic applications as they can lead to time-inconsistent preferences \cite{krepsPorteus,epsteinZin1}. However, this specific form of the preferences using an exponential and no discounting factor, is time-consistent (see \cite{epsteinZin1}).
We do not need to include a discount factor because incorporating mortality in
the preferences already provides an incentive for earlier consumption. We refer
to this preference model (with arbitrary $u$) as exponential Kihlstrom--Mirman (EKM) preferences.

Similar to Epstein--Zin preferences, our preference model includes separate
parameters determining risk and satiation. Existing research 
suggests that separate parameters are necessary to resolve observed asset pricing puzzles \cite{bansalYaron,bansal,benzoniEtAl,bhamraEtAl}. This strongly suggests that the preferences of members of our fund will also require separate parameters for risk and satiation. However, unlike Epstein--Zin preferences, our preferences do not require a recursive computation of the utility in terms of conditional expectations at each time point. This makes the utility function \eqref{eq:utility} much simpler to evaluate than Epstein--Zin preferences. As a result, our choice of
preferences is well-suited to a machine-learning approach which will require rapid
computation of this utility.

To compute this utility function, we assume that consumption and individual longevity risk are independent. We also assume there is no systematic longevity risk and that the probability an individual dies in a given year $s$ is given by $\overline{p}_s$.
\begin{equation}
    U = -\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Invest}} \left[ \sum_{s=t_{\RA}}^T \overline{p}_s\, \text{exp}\left(-\alpha\sum_{t=t_{\RA}}^{s}  u(c_t,a) \delta t\right) \right].
\end{equation}
In this formula, ${\mathbb E}_\mathrm{Invest}$ denotes the expectation across investment scenarios
and so excludes the mortality component of our probability model, which is accounted for by the term ${\overline{p}}_s$. $T$ is the maximum time of death, which is finite for the mortality model we are using. If we generate $N$ investment scenarios and label the consumption in each case $c^{(j)}$ with $1\leq j \leq N$, we may estimate the utility function using the following expression

\begin{equation}
    \hat{U}:=-\frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N \left[ \sum_{s=t_{\RA}}^T \overline{p}_s\, \text{exp}\left(-\alpha\sum_{t=t_{\RA}}^{s}  u(c_t^{(j)},a) \delta t \right) \right].
    \label{eq:utility}
\end{equation}


%We find the optimal strategy to minimize this loss function using a neural network approach. 
Since our EKM utility function is inhomogeneous, maximising it
using traditional PDE techniques could be computationally demanding. This is because
we do not benefit from the dimension reduction that occurs from using homogeneous preferences. 
As such, we have chosen to use machine learning, specifically a recurrent neural network, to find the optimal strategy that maximises this utility function. In this setting, the problem can be formulated straightforwardly as requiring the network to learn the controls that maximise the utility function $\hat{U}$. We give technical details on the training and use of our network in Appendix \ref{appendix:neuralNetworkDesign}.

We take $L=\log(-\hat{U})$ to be the loss function
for our machine learning model, so that minimising $L$ is equivalent to maximising $\hat{U}$. The $\log$ transform is chosen to avoid excessively large loss values. First note that we may write
\begin{align*}
    -\hat{U} &= \frac{1}{N}\sum^N_{j=1}\sum_{s=t_{\RA}}^T \exp\left(\text{log}(\tilde{p}_s)-\alpha\sum^s_{t=t_{\RA}}u(c_{t}^{(j)}, a) \delta t\right)\\
    & = \frac{1}{N}\sum^N_{j=1}\text{exp}\left(\text{log}\left(\sum_{s=t_{\RA}}^T \exp\left(\text{log}(\tilde{p}_s)-\alpha \sum^s_{t=t_{\RA}}u(c_{t}^{(j)}, a) \delta t\right)\right)\right).
\end{align*}
Hence, our loss function is given by
\begin{multline}\label{eq:loss}
    L = \log\left(\sum^N_{j=1}\exp\left(\log\left(\sum_{s=t_{\RA}}^T \exp\left(\log(\tilde{p}_s)-\alpha \sum^s_{t=t_{\RA}}u(c_{t}^{(j)}, a) \delta t\right)\right)\right)\right)\\
    - \log(N).
\end{multline}
We then evaluate this expression using a $\logsumexp$ function to avoid excessive rounding errors.


One particular advantage of the neural network approach is that it is very easy to change
our loss function to include additional features such as a preference for smoother retirement incomes. We accept that it is very difficult to know \textit{a priori} what might be a sensible choice
for a loss function. Our philosophy has been to simply experiment with different possibilities and parameter values until we identified a loss function which we felt met our needs. Our specific choices were motivated by looking for a loss function which we felt gave an ``income for life'', which could be rationally justified and which was easy to compare with the output of a shared-indexation CDC scheme.

\subsection{Effectiveness of the internal longevity market}

Our simulations in the previous section assume an infinite fund size. In this section,
we investigate how large schemes need to be for the longevity market to be effective. The
key observation is that what matters is the overall size of the longevity market, and not the size of the individual schemes. As a result, it is possible to have a large number of heterogeneous, individually small schemes and still obtain near-perfect elimination of individual
longevity risk.

To illustrate this, we simulate a sequence of collective-drawdown plans each containing 20 members. Within each plan, all members have the same age, investment and consumption strategy. We create a sequence of plans, each representing a different cohort of members. In our simulations, we treat each of these plans as though they are a separate scheme. This simulation can therefore be interpreted as both an example of how a collective-drawdown scheme might operate for a single employer with finite fund size, and as an example of how multiple small, demographically distinct schemes can effectively share a longevity market.

Some care is required to apply the strategy for an infinite fund to a finite fund. If this is done naively, the neural network can lose track of a member's wealth as the network does not receive any input providing data on how mortality has differed from central projections. To account for this, we adjust the equity risk-factors that are fed into the network to account for the noise in longevity credits which would otherwise be hidden from the network. 
Full details on how this is performed are given in Appendix \ref{sec:appendixFiniteFund}.

The result for the first generation in our simulation is shown in Figure \ref{fig:finiteScheme} and is compared to the results obtained using an infinite fund. We perform 10000 simulations
to obtain these plots and only show deciles where there are at least 100 scenarios containing a survivor of the given age. These plots show that the outcomes for a finite fund with 20 members in each generation.

Up to age 95, outcomes are essentially indistinguishable from the outcomes in an infinite fund.
The outcomes achieved from 95 onwards are somewhat below those of an infinite fund, but still outperform the shared-indexation CDC fund. One could attempt to tune the network further to take account of
the fact that the longevity market is less effective once one is making large contributions. For example, if there were a cap on the maximum contribution to the longevity pool, this could be accounted for when training the network.

\section{Additional considerations when comparing shared-indexation and collective-drawdown}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Optimality}


One criticism of investment approaches based on utility functions is that the true
utility function of any investor is unknown. Nevertheless, using a rational choice of 
utility function as a basis
of the design of a fund still has the advantage that one can guarantee that it will be impossible to find any alternative design which is unequivocally better (in the sense that it stochastically dominates the strategy found using the utility function). Thus, while one may debate the relative merits of two strategies found using different utility functions, they will not produce entirely irrational strategies.

By contrast, the flat-accrual shared-indexation CDC scheme considered in \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly}, is unequivocally worse than shared-indexation schemes with dynamic-accrual from the point of view of individuals in the steady-state of these schemes.
It is just about possible to argue that some people may prefer the outcomes of the standard dynamic-accrual scheme illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:mainResult}, but we feel that the collective-drawdown scheme gives obviously better results except in the most pedantic sense. We hypothesize that if one were to artificially design a loss function that allows for decreasing income in retirement, it would be possible to identify a strategy that stochastically dominates the shared-indexation scheme.

Our philosophy is that, although one may not know one's utility function \textit{a priori}, one could look at a menu of possible outcomes coming from a variety of utility functions and thereby identify a reasonable choice to be used in optimization problems. Indeed, we found the parameter values for our loss function by this process, visually selecting for a graph that we felt most people would agree outperforms the shared-indexation CDC fund.

In a complete market, where arbitrary derivatives on any risk-factors can be purchased,
it is not possible for any group of individuals (subject to minor assumptions on their preferences) to agree any mutually beneficial contracts. A precise statement is given in Theorem \ref{prop:noGoTheorem} in the appendix. The proof is not difficult, but giving a precise statement requires using
the technical vocabulary of mathematical probability theory.
The key assumptions are: there are a finite number of members; at the time a member agrees to join the scheme, it is always in their best interests to do so; additional wealth results in strictly better outcomes. The first assumption rules out Ponzi-type schemes which rely on an infinite time horizon. The second assumption rules out strategies where one invests in risky assets on behalf of an individual before they are able to consent. The second assumption also rules out central-planner approaches where some individuals lose out but some overall social utility function is maximized. The third assumption rules out situations where a member is indifferent to having their wealth distributed to others. 

If the provider is reasonably sized, the internal insurance market will be sufficiently
effective that we can model individual longevity risk as being perfectly-insurable. The Black--Scholes model is well-known to be a complete market model. The end result is a complete market in
both investment and longevity risk factors.
As a result, Theorem \ref{prop:noGoTheorem} tells us that the optimal strategy for a heterogeneous collective of individuals in the Black--Scholes model is for each of them to pursue the investment and consumption strategy they would follow in an infinite collective of like-minded individuals. What this means
is that in complete market models, the only possible benefit of collective pensions
is longevity insurance.


In an incomplete market, Theorem \ref{prop:noGoTheorem} does not apply. As a result,
the investment strategy found using a fund of identical
individuals will not be optimal. In an incomplete market it would be theoretically possible to set
up an internal insurance market in risk-factors which are not currently traded. If
members are heterogeneous, then they will have different views on the value of this insurance and as a result, they will be able to trade in insurance for mutual benefit. This idea is explored in \cite{armstrong_dalby} for the case of systematic longevity risk, where the maximal possible benefit of mutual insurance against this risk factor is computed. However, except for this single example, it is currently unknown how to practically compute optimal mutual insurance strategies. Therefore, for the time being, the best available approach is to use the strategy found for an infinite number of identical individuals pooling longevity risk via an internal insurance market only. Other possible benefits of collective funds in incomplete markets include the reduction of transaction costs through investment pooling. This may be particularly useful if some scheme members wish to take leveraged positions, but the fund as a whole does not require leverage.

Theorem \ref{prop:noGoTheorem} provides a useful sanity check on the plausibility of
proposed strategies for managing collective funds. If the scheme
design does not explain how mutual insurance
in untraded risk factors is used to obtain mutual benefit, then the effectiveness of the scheme
must depend on breaking some other assumption of the theorem, not the complete market hypothesis.



%One way to design collective schemes that violates the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:noGoTheorem} is to use a central planner, who chooses an overall objective. Such a scheme may deliberately redistribute wealth from rich to poor if the social planner believes this is preferable, and this might be a perfectly appropriate design for a state pension scheme. However, in the UK private pensions market, members should be allowed to opt out of their scheme and the central-planning approach relies upon either compulsion, altruism or ignorance.

%Another way scheme designs may violate the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:noGoTheorem} is to use an infinite time-horizon to construct a form of Ponzi scheme, with later generations subsidizing earlier generations. Regulators should ensure that schemes operate effectively on finite time-horizons and, if necessary, put money aside to ensure that schemes can be shut down without later generations losing out.

We would argue that a regulator should insist upon a mathematically rigorous explanation of how any proposed collective scheme operates that explains how its performance can be understood in the light of Theorem \ref{thm:noGoTheorem}.


\subsection{Member communications}

An important function of the member layer in our architecture is communication.
In a collective-drawdown scheme, the total asset value of each member is known at all times. However, this does not necessarily mean this figure should be automatically communicated to members. There are strong arguments that it is better for members to focus on their benefit in retirement rather than on their pot size \cite{mertonCrisis}.

As a result, one might design member communications in a CDC scheme to inform members about projected, real-terms future benefits. There are, of course, challenges in how to convey the complex information about uncertainty and future growth in a fashion that will be understood by members, but this is a common problem in most designs. Defined-benefit approaches can avoid these issues, but only by sacrificing optimality.

It may be tempting in shared-indexation CDC designs to inform members about nominal entitlements, but we believe this would be misleading as members are likely to confuse projected, real-terms future benefits with their nominal benefit. The nominal benefit figure on its own without considering the level of indexation is an essentially meaningless number. Directly informing members of their nominal benefit and the level of indexation would require members to have a detailed understanding of the shared-indexation approach which seems unrealistic. We therefore believe that it is better to only inform members of shared-indexation schemes of their projected, real-terms future benefits. This requires stochastic modelling of the future evolution of the fund. 

\subsection{Investment choice}

It is generally accepted that in most occupational pension schemes, members will
simply accept the default investment decisions that are given to them. It is for this
reason that we have proposed that strategic decisions are made at the employer level,
rather than by the individual members.

Nevertheless, it is worth noting that our design is considerably more flexible than
shared-indexation CDC as one does not require large collections of identical individuals in
any scheme, simply a large number of members overall participating in the insurance market. As a result, an employer could offer a number of tailored investment options in much
the same way as DC funds currently offer different investment choices for individuals with different risk appetites. Members could be guided to choose from a menu of options
in just the same way as DC funds currently guide investors.

It is also possible, in principle, to set up a bespoke strategy for a single member and,
using the internal longevity insurance, provide them with outcomes that are equivalent to
those they could obtain in a fund containing an infinite number of like-minded individuals.
This opens up the possibility of offering a form of self-invested personal pension (SIPP)
which benefits from longevity pooling. The principle issue would be the
individual underwriting required.

\subsection{Interpretability}

It is important to consider how easy it is to understand the operation of
any given scheme design. As a result, one may have reservations about using a neural network to choose investment and consumption strategies.

We would agree that if one can find a closed-form formula for the investment and 
consumption decisions of a network that yields similar outcomes to our strategy, this would
be preferable. It seems likely that this will be possible in the simplified Black--Scholes model, as we have already seen the consumption strategy appears to be essentially deterministic. However, in a realistic stochastic model, one would expect to
have to choose between interpretability and optimality.

Although a closed form formula has some advantages, a closed-form formula for investment and consumption may not, in practice, be particularly easy to interpret. Shared-indexation CDC schemes provide a case in point. Despite the closed-form formulae describing the scheme's operation, one has little insight into
what the resulting retirement outcomes will be, except through simulation.

Within a neural network, the precise behaviour of the network is hard to understand because it depends on the precise values of a large number of parameters. However, the behaviour of a shared-indexation CDC fund also depends on a large number of variables, specifically the liabilities that have developed over time. This makes the income received from a shared-indexation fund a form of path-dependent derivative, and means that to compute the value of the pension one receives in return for a particular contribution, one must perform a Monte Carlo simulation.

While there is no simple formula for the investment and consumption decisions that 
the neural network approach will make, it does have the clear advantage that the market value of the pension an individual purchases each year will exactly match their contribution. In this important sense, collective-drawdown schemes are more interpretable than a shared-indexation design.

A further advantage of the collective-drawdown approach is that the objective function is
highly interpretable, with the parameters controlling risk-appetite, satiation and adequacy. The available control parameters in a shared-indexation CDC scheme (the proportion invested in risky assets, the value of $h_{\min}$ and the value of $h_{\max}$) are not connected directly to preferences and this makes their impact harder to understand.

Moreover, the motivation for the use of shared-indexation rather than seeking optimality is obscure. We believe that the central attraction of shared-indexation CDC design is that it
allows a transfer of risk between generations to occur, while superficially making this appear fair.
Clause 17.4 (c) of the legislation governing the operation of CDC funds requires that benefit adjustments ``must be
applied to all the members of the scheme without variation''
 \cite{cdcRegulations}.
To clarify the meaning of this, let us suppose that each individual $i$ has a promised income stream $c^i_t$ at each future time $t$. If in a benefit adjustment, each individual were now to receive the quantity $(1+h)c^i_t$ for some $h$, this could be reasonably described as a fair distribution of investment risk among members. We believe that this is how most people would interpret 17.4 (c). However, in shared-indexation CDC funds, 17.4 (c) really means that each individual receives an adjusted income stream of $(1+h)^t c^i_t$, until death at time $t$. This compounding means that any changes in indexation are felt much more strongly by younger generations, resulting in a transfer of risk from old to young. %This argument is also why people believe shared-indexation ``smooths pensions". However, as \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly} shows, the inaccuracy of the benefit pricing formula for calculating $h$, means smoothing only occurs once a member retires as a result of the lifestyling investment strategy. 
The language used to describe the operation of shared-indexation CDC funds, including in legislation, obscures this intended transfer of risk.

A further advantage of collective-drawdown schemes, is that one does not
need to model the behaviour of other members joining and leaving the scheme. The 
internal longevity market will function effectively across a broad range of possibilities for fund composition. By contrast, modelling the details of fund composition and the changing levels of liabilities are essential in shared-indexation schemes. For example, shared-indexation schemes behave very differently at startup and during closure than they do in their long-term steady state. Moreover, modelling the future demographics of an employer is extremely challenging. As a result, members of shared-indexation schemes are subject to hard-to-quantify risks from events such as scheme closure or changing demographics.

This has an impact on how easy it is to test different strategies in simulations.
If the outcome of a particular scheme design can only be known through simulation, then the depth of testing which a scheme has undergone is of paramount importance.
One can obtain a good understanding of the behaviour of a collective-drawdown fund
by simulating a single infinite cohort. By contrast, to understand a shared-indexation fund, one must simulate all generations over a long time period. This makes it much more computationally costly to simulate shared-indexation funds than collective-drawdown funds. Because of the ease of simulating collective-drawdown funds, we have been able to perform robust tests to check that our network performs correctly. Details of testing measures can be found in \Cref{sec:testing}. In \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly}, it is shown that testing the approximate pricing methodologies and heuristic strategies used in shared-indexation funds is extremely challenging,
since there is little theoretical understanding of what to expect. The difficulty of testing shared-indexation funds may explain why the scale of intergenerational cross-subsidies reported in \cite{armstrong_dalby_donnelly} were not known by industry.

In summary, we argue that the claimed simplicity of shared-indexation CDC schemes is
largely illusory and that collective-drawdown schemes have numerous interpretability advantages
over shared-indexation CDC. Nevertheless, interpretability issues will always remain in 
any scheme design, and this makes thorough testing and independent scrutiny essential
features of any design.


\subsection{Transfers in and out}

Transferring in and out of a shared-indexation scheme is complicated, as it is unclear
how to compute transfer values. By contrast, the value of an individual's assets in an
collective-drawdown scheme are always known.

The principle concern in a collective-drawdown scheme (which also exists in a shared-indexation scheme), is that if an individual obtains information about their health, they may wish to withdraw from the scheme. Considering this question in detail would require a model for 
how information about one's health is likely to arrive, and to what extent such information narrows the uncertainty around time of death. Modelling this is beyond the scope of this paper, but would be an interesting topic for further research.

In lieu of this, a pragmatic solution is to allow individuals to opt out of the pension up to retirement, but not after. In this case, individuals would not participate in the longevity pool until retirement, and as a result, could leave a bequest if they die before retirement.

This crude solution may be unnecessarily restrictive. It would seem reasonable to allow members to leave after retirement, if they give sufficient notice to prevent them using this as a mechanism to exploit private information. One might then need to adjust the longevity estimates for members of a scheme to condition on the fact that they have not left. One might also consider performing custom underwriting that would allow the member to remain in the scheme. By using custom underwriting and the correct probabilities for the internal longevity market, one could adjust the individual's investment and consumption strategy to better match their new circumstances.
 


\section{Conclusions}\label{sec:conclusions}

In complete market models, collective-drawdown schemes combined with an internal
market for individual longevity-risk can provide optimal outcomes for investors. Such
schemes have a number of other advantages over alternative approaches to managing
collective pensions, such as enabling individual investment choice.

In incomplete markets, it may be possible to obtain even better schemes by creating
additional internal markets. It remains to be seen whether the benefits of this approach
will justify the additional complexity of operation and member communications.

The design of collective-drawdown schemes does not require pre-committing to using a particular strategy for all time. So, in the event that better strategies can be found using other forms of mutual insurance, there should be no obstacle to adopting them in future.

In future work, we will focus on the robustness and realism of outcomes from our collective-drawdown fund by: enabling the network to learn optimal strategies for a range of parameter values so real-time comparisons of strategies can be made, include additional terms in our loss function to induce a preference for smoothness in pension outcomes, and including a more realistic economic model with more asset classes and bond investment strategies that match those used in the pensions industry.

\section{Neural Network Design}
\label{appendix:neuralNetworkDesign}

\subsection{Network architecture and implementation}

Our machine learning code base is built in Python using the Tensorflow package.
We use a recurrent neural network consisting of six layers: 
\begin{itemize}
    \item The first input layer has 2 nodes, representing the increments of a Brownian motion driving a stock price process and the current time $t$.

    \item The second layer is a dense layer with 32 nodes and a ReLU activation function.

    \item The third layer is a gated recurrent unit (GRU) with 10 nodes. This is the recurrent layer in our network. The activation function is the hyperbolic tangent function and the recurrent activation function is sigmoid. This layer allows us to deal with the time dependent nature of our data. The GRU is set up so as to return an output at each time point, hence the final layer returns predictions at each time point.
    
    \item The fourth and fifth layers are identical to the second layer.

    \item The final output layer has 2 nodes, which represent the two predictions the network must make, the quantity to invest in a risky asset and the proportion of wealth to consume. Because of the way the GRU is used, we therefore obtain investment and consumption decisions in each year of our simulation. Consumption before retirement is ignored by our loss function.

\end{itemize}
\noindent
We used the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.001. Training was carried out over 20 epochs, each consisting of 10,000 scenarios with a batch size of 100. A validation set of 10,000 separately generated scenarios was evaluated at the end of each epoch. This gave the strategies in \Cref{sec:results}.

\subsection{Training Data}

We trained our network to find the optimal investment and consumption strategy within a Black--Scholes model. We therefore suppose that the price of the risky asset, $S$, follows a geometric Brownian motion
\begin{equation}
    \ed S_t = \mu S_t \ed t + \sigma S_t \, \ed W_t, \label{eq:BSM}
\end{equation}
where $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ is the growth rate, $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$ the volatility and $W$ a standard Brownian motion.

We assume that consumption and investment decisions occur at times ${\cal T}:=\{0,\delta t, 2 \delta t, \ldots \}$. Between these
times we pursue a fixed-weight strategy. Let $\pi_t$
denote the investment proportion chosen at a time $t \in {\cal T}$. We suppose that we hold this proportion
of our wealth in stocks for all $s \in [t,t+\delta t)$
with the remainder in a riskless asset that grows at rate $r$. The wealth satisfies the stochastic differential equation (SDE)
\begin{equation}
    \ed w_s = w_s(\pi_t \mu + (1-\pi_t)r)\ed s + w_s \pi_t \sigma \, \ed W_s.\label{eq:returns}
\end{equation}
on the interval $[w_t, w_{t+\delta t})$. We will write
$w_{(t+\delta t)-}$ for the left limit of this process.
By Ito's lemma, we can derive the log wealth process. That is
\begin{equation}
    \ed (\log(w_s)) = \left(\pi_t \mu + (1-\pi_t)r-\frac{1}{2}(\pi_t\sigma)^2 \right)\ed s + \pi_t\sigma \ed W_s.\label{eq:log_sde}
\end{equation}
So we
have
\begin{equation}
    \log(w_{(t+\delta t)-}) - \log(w_t) = \left(\pi_t \mu + (1-\pi_t)r-\frac{1}{2}(\pi_t\sigma)^2 \right) \delta t + \pi_t\sigma (W_{t+\delta t}-W_t).
\end{equation}
We make the definition
\[
\epsilon_t := \frac{W_{t+\delta t}-W_t}{\sqrt{\delta t}}, %=
\]
so $\epsilon_t$ follows a standard normal distribution.
Note, that our approach of using fixed-weight strategies over each period ensures that strategies that put one into debt are automatically eliminated.  

We use these normally distributed increments $\epsilon_t$ as the input to our neural network. The outputs of our neural network represent  $c_t\in[0, 1]$, the proportion of wealth consumed at time $t$, and the proportion invested in a risky asset at time $t$, $\pi_t\in\mathbb{R}$.
The value of the output representing $c_t$ is simply ignored for $t<t_{\RA}$.


Define a function $F$ to compute
the log returns over each interval by
\[
F(\pi,\epsilon):=
\left(\pi \mu + (1-\pi)r-\frac{1}{2}(\pi \sigma)^2 \right) \delta t+ \pi \sigma \epsilon \sqrt{ \delta t}.
\]
so that
\[
w_{t-}=\exp(F(\pi_{t-\delta t}, \epsilon_{t-\delta t})) w_{t-\delta t} 
\]
Contributions are a fixed proportion of salary $s_t$, given by $\alpha s_t$. We consider an infinite fund of identical individuals, so the longevity payment $P_{\infty,t}$, is given by
\begin{equation}
    P_{\infty,t} w_{t-} := \left( \frac{p_t}{1-p_t} \right) w_{t-},\label{eq:payment}
\end{equation}
where $p_t$ is the probability of dying this year given you were alive last year.
This payment is received after the first year of retirement i.e., we assume everyone survives to age 65 and can die from age 66 onward. Thus, the wealth in year $t$ after payments and consumption satisfies
\begin{equation}
    w_{t} = \alpha s_t \mathbbm{1}_{t<t_{\RA}} + (1- c_t
    \mathbbm{1}_{t\geq t_{\RA}})(1+ P_{\infty,t} \mathbbm{1}_{t>t_{\RA}}  )w_{t-},
\label{eq:wealthInfinite}    
\end{equation}
where $\mathbbm{1}$ denotes an indicator function.

All that remains is to compute the replacement ratio during decumulation. Recall, the replacement ratio is defined to be the proportion of final salary indexed by inflation that a consumption stream provides. We call this indexation the replacement level $L_t$. At the start of retirement, $L_{t_{\RA}}=s_{t_{\RA}-1}$ i.e., an individuals final salary. In subsequent years,
\begin{equation}
    L_{t+1}=L_{t}(1+i),
\end{equation}
where $i$ denotes the level of inflation. 

We can now define the replacement ratio at time $t \in [t_{\RA}, T]$ as
\begin{equation}
    R_{t}=\frac{c_t w_t}{L_{t}}.
\end{equation}
The replacement vector, $(R_{t_{\RA}}, \ldots,R_{T})$, where $T$ is the year we declare everyone to be deceased and end the simulation, is then put into our loss function \eqref{eq:loss} and the gradient update is computed accordingly.


\subsection{Using the neural network in a finite fund}
\label{sec:appendixFiniteFund}

Although the network has been trained on the assumption that the fund is infinite,
in practice it will, of course, be finite. When we use the neural network to choose
investment and consumption decisions for our simulation, we modify the input representing the noise term to take account of this discrepancy. In our calculation below, $\tilde{\epsilon}_t$ will be the input used for the neural network, whereas $\epsilon_t$ will represent the actual stock increments.

%The issue is that our network is not given the current wealth as an input. Instead, the network must calculate this state information implicitly using its recurrent layers to keep a memory of this state.

The idea is to include the noise coming from
the stochastic longevity payments in the computation
of $\tilde{\epsilon}_t$, so that a neural network trained on the assumption that equation \eqref{eq:wealthInfinite} holds, will still 
correctly compute the total wealth. The true longevity payment for a finite fund is a random variable
which we denote by $P_{f,t} w_{t-}$. In a finite fund, the wealth satisfies the following modified version of equation \eqref{eq:wealthInfinite}.
\begin{equation}
    w_{t} = \alpha s_t \mathbbm{1}_{t<t_{\RA}} + (1 - c_t
    \mathbbm{1}_{t\geq t_{\RA}} )(1+ P_{f,t} \mathbbm{1}_{t>t_{\RA}})w_{t-}.
\label{eq:wealthFinite}    
\end{equation}

Comparing equations \eqref{eq:wealthFinite} and \eqref{eq:wealthInfinite}, we define the modified noise process $\tilde{\epsilon}_t$ by requiring that the following equation holds
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
(1 + P_{f,t} \mathbbm{1}_{t>t_{\RA}}) &\exp(F(\pi_{t-\delta t}, \epsilon_{t-\delta t})) w_{t-\delta t} \\
    &=
(1 + P_{\infty,t} \mathbbm{1}_{t>t_{\RA}})  \exp(F(\pi_{t-\delta t}, \tilde{\epsilon}_{t-\delta t})) w_{t-\delta t}.    
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
When we pass $\tilde{\epsilon}_t$ as the noise input into the neural network which has been trained assuming an infinite fund, it
will compute the wealth of the fund at the next period
so that it matches that given by equation \eqref{eq:wealthFinite}.




\section{Proof that there are no mutually beneficial contracts in complete markets}

Let ${\cal T} \subseteq \R$ be a finite set of time points. Let
$(\Omega, {\cal F}, ({\cal F}_t)_{t \in {\cal T}}, {\mathbb P})$ be a filtered probability space. We write $L^0(X,{\cal F}_t)$ for the set of ${\cal F}_t$-measurable
$X$-valued random variables. Given $s \in {\cal T}$,
we write ${\cal T}_{\geq s} := \{ t \in {\cal T} \mid t\geq s\}$.
We write ${\cal P}_{\geq s}$ for the the space of adapted
$\R$-valued processes $(\gamma)_{t \in {\cal T}_{\geq s}}$.


We assume that there is a complete market, so we can find
a numeraire asset $N$ and a measure ${\mathbb Q}$ equivalent to ${\mathbb P}$, such that given $s \in {\cal T}$ and $\gamma$ in ${\cal P}_{\geq s}$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
E_{\mathbb Q} \left( \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{\geq s}} \max\{{\gamma}_t, 0\} \mid {\cal F}_s \right) < \infty,
\label{eq:minusInfinity}
\end{equation}
it is possible to purchase the sequence of cashflows $(\gamma_t N_t)_{t \in \cal T}$ at time $s$ for the price
\[
E_{\mathbb Q}\left( \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{\geq s}} \gamma_t \mid {\cal F}_s \right).
\]
We write ${\cal P}_{\geq s, \infty}$ for the set of $\gamma \in {\cal P}_{\geq s}$ satisfying equation \eqref{eq:minusInfinity}.

We suppose that there are $n$ individuals. Individual $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$)
is able to make decisions on their participation in a pension scheme from time
$t_i \in {\cal T}$. We write ${\cal T}_i:={\cal T}_{\geq t_i}$ and ${\cal P}_{i}:={\cal P}_{\geq t_i}$.

Individual $i$'s preferences over income streams are given by a map
\[
r_i: {\cal P}_{i} \times {\cal P}_{i} \to L^0(\{1,0\}; {\cal F}_{t_i} ).
\]
Given $\gamma_1, \gamma_2 \in {\cal P}_{i}$, we will write $({\gamma_1} <_i {\gamma_2})(\omega)$ if
$r_i(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)(\omega)=1$. Thus $\gamma_1 <_i \gamma_2$ is a boolean-valued
random variable. If $\gamma_1 <_i \gamma_2$ then this is interpreted as meaning
that at time $t_i$, individual $i$ prefers receiving the cashflows $((\gamma_2)_t N_t)_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}}$ to receiving the cashflows $((\gamma_1)_t N_t)_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}}$.

We will assume two axioms for this preference relation.
\begin{axiom}{A}
The relationship $<_i$ is almost-surely a total order on ${\cal P}_{i}$.
\end{axiom}

To state our next axiom we need to introduce an additional concept.
\begin{definition}
Define $m_i:{\cal P}_{i} \to L^0(\{1,0\}; {\cal F}_{t_i} )$ by
\[
m_i(\gamma)(\omega)=\begin{cases}
0 & \exists \;\tilde{\gamma} \in {\cal P}_{i} \;\text{ such that }\; ({\tilde{\gamma} <_i \gamma})(\omega); \\
1 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
When $m_i(\gamma)=1$, we say that $\gamma$ is minimal for $i$.
\end{definition}
We have in mind situations where preferences are determined by a concave
gain function such as an expected utility which takes values in ${\mathbb R} \cup \{-\infty\}$. When the expected utility of $\gamma$ is equal to $\{ -\infty \}$, we would have that $\gamma$ is minimal. This motivates our next axiom, which essentially states
that additional wealth always improves one's situation unless one's situation is ``infinitely bad''.

\begin{axiom}{B}
Let $\epsilon$ be an ${\cal F}_{t_i}$-measurable real
random variable. Suppose $\gamma \in {\cal P}_{i}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb P}( (\gamma + \epsilon >_i \gamma) \text{ or } (\gamma \text{ is minimal for $i$}) {\text{ or }}(\epsilon\leq 0))=1 .
\end{equation*}
\end{axiom}
Our next axiom assumes that cashflows with infinitely negative market value are
unacceptable to all individuals.
\begin{axiom}{C}
If $\gamma \in {\cal P}_{\geq t_i,-\infty}$ then $\gamma$ is almost surely minimal for $i$.
\end{axiom}

We now suppose that each individual, $i$, has an income stream represented by $\eta^i \in {\cal P}_{i}$. The value of this income stream is given by $(\eta^i_t N_t)_{t \in {{\cal T}_{i}}}$.
We assume it is of finite value, so 
\[
E_{\mathbb Q}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \eta^i_t\right)<\infty \quad \text{a.s.} 
\]
\begin{definition}
An income stream $\gamma \in {\cal P}_i$ is {\em available} to investor $i$ if
\begin{equation}
E_{\mathbb Q}\left( \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \gamma_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i}\right) \leq 
E_{\mathbb Q}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \eta^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right)<\infty .
\label{eq:availability}
\end{equation}
The availability of $\gamma$ is a boolean-valued random variable.
\end{definition}
Since we are working in a complete market, this is a reasonable definition. It is in making this definition that
we are assuming a complete market.

A strategy for an individual investor
is represented by an element of ${\cal P}_{i}$ and so
may depend on any  information available at time $t_i$.

\begin{definition}
Given $\gamma \in {\cal P}_0$ and a strategy $\tilde{\gamma} \in {\cal P}_{i}$ for investor $i$, we will say
that $\tilde{\gamma}$ {\em sometimes outperforms} $\gamma$ if
\[
{\mathbb P}( \gamma <_i \tilde{\gamma} \text{ and $\tilde\gamma$ is available to $i$} )>0.
\]
\end{definition}

In a collective scheme, a strategy is formed at time $0$ for all investors and so is represented by an element $\gamma \in \Pi_{i=1}^n {\cal P}_{i}$ whose components $\gamma^i$ represent the cashflow given to investor $i$.
This strategy is affordable if and only if
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb Q}\left( \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \gamma^i_t \right)
\leq \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb Q}\left( \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \eta^i_t \right).
\label{eq:collectiveConstraint}
\end{equation}

If joining the collective is not compulsory, at time $t_i$, individual $i$ will not join the collective if they can obtain a better income stream by investing directly.
This motivates the next definition.
\begin{definition}
A $\gamma \in \Pi_{i=1}^n {\cal P}_{i}$ is {\em viable}
if there does not exist a pair $(i,\tilde{\gamma})$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$ and $\tilde{\gamma} \in {\cal P}_{i}$, where $\tilde{\gamma}$ sometimes outperforms $\gamma^i$ for investor $i$.
\end{definition}
We may now state our main result.
\begin{theorem}
\label{prop:noGoTheorem}
If $\gamma \in \Pi_{i=1}^n {\cal P}_{i}$
is viable and satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{eq:collectiveConstraint},
then either:
\begin{enumerate}
\item there exists an individual $i$ for whom $\gamma^i$ is minimal with non-zero probability;
\item $\gamma^i$ is almost-surely available to individual $i$ for all $i$ ($1\leq i \leq n$).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We will suppose that for each individual $i$, $\gamma^i$ is almost surely not minimal,
and will prove that the second condition must then hold.

Since $\gamma^i$ is almost surely not minimal, we have by Axiom C
that $\gamma^i \notin {\cal P}_{\geq t_i,-\infty}.$

We first show that for all $i$
\begin{equation}
{\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \gamma^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right)
\geq {\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \eta^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right) \text{ a.s.}
\label{eq:reverseEquality}
\end{equation}
Suppose for contradiction that 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\left[
{\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \gamma^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right)
< {\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \eta^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right)
\right]>0.
\label{eq:positiveProbAssumption}
\end{equation}
Define
\[
\epsilon =
f \left[ \frac{ {\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \eta^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i}  \right)-{\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_{i}} \gamma^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right)}{2 |{\cal T}_{i}|} \right] ,
\]
where
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
0  & \ x \leq 0 \\
\frac{1}{x} & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Note, that $\epsilon$ is ${\cal F}_{t_i}$-measurable.
By Axiom B, we know that $\gamma^i <_i \gamma^i + \epsilon$ almost surely whenever
$\gamma^i$ is available to investor $i$. The strategy $\tilde{\gamma}=\gamma+\epsilon(\omega)$ will sometimes outperform
$\gamma^i$, by \eqref{eq:positiveProbAssumption}. This contradicts the assumption
that $\gamma$ is viable.

We have now established that \eqref{eq:reverseEquality} holds.
It then follows that
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}\left( \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \gamma^i_t  \right)
\geq {\mathbb E}\left( \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \eta^i_t \right).
\end{equation*}

Since $\gamma^i \notin {\cal P}_{\geq t_i,-\infty}$, this is an inequality in finite numbers. It follows
that
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \gamma^i_t \right)
\geq {\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \eta^i_t \right).
\end{equation*}
Hence, by equation \eqref{eq:collectiveConstraint}, we must have equality throughout,
including equation \eqref{eq:reverseEquality}.
Thus
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \gamma^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right)
\leq {\mathbb E}\left(\sum_{t \in {\cal T}_i} \eta^i_t \mid {\cal F}_{t_i} \right),
\end{equation*}
Thus $\gamma^i$ is available to individual $i$.
\end{proof}



\section{Testing}\label{sec:testing}
To test that our model trains adequately and that the code which feeds it is correct, we perform three important checks. 

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Given a lifestyling and inflation linked annuity purchase strategy, we find our replacement ratio and final wealth calculations produce a constant income in retirement with a final wealth of zero, as expected.

    \item We test that our method of training the neural network can reproduce the strategy and value function (at time 0), for the classical Merton problem. That is, maximising consumption over a given time horizon. For discrete time consumption and continuous time investment, the analytical solution can be found in \cite{armstrong_buescu_dalby} Theorem 2.2. Since we simulate log returns on the asset, which follows a constant coefficient SDE, our approximation should be exact. We find that we can reproduce the optimal solution to the Merton problem.

    \item We test that our method of training the neural network can reproduce the strategy and value function (at time 0), for maximising von-Neumann Morgernstern utility with mortality %That is, maximising
    %\begin{equation}   
    %    \E\left( \sum_{t \in {\cal T}, t \leq \tau } c_t^\alpha \right),
    %\end{equation}
    for discrete-time consumption and continuous-time investment. The analytical solution can again be found in \cite{armstrong_buescu_dalby} Theorem 2.2. We find that we can reproduce the optimal solution to this problem.
\end{enumerate}
This suggests our codebase deals with strategies, consumption, investment and mortality correctly, all of which feed into the maximisation of the utility function described in \Cref{sec:loss}.

title: Influence and information in a collective of self-propelled particles
summary:
While information-theoretic quantities, such as transfer entropy, have been
widely adopted to infer causal relationships in collective systems, a critical
gap exists: the absence of quantitative evidence directly linking
information-theoretic quantities to a physically defined influence. This letter
addresses this gap by proposing a modified Vicsek model that enables the
calculation of a physically interpretable influence grounded in the angular
interactions between particles. Averaged pairwise influences can serve as new
order parameters to indicate collective phase transitions. We reveal
quantitative relations between information, represented by transfer entropy,
and average influence in pairwise and collective interactions. We test three
typical methods of partial information decomposition and find that the method
based on intrinsic mutual information gives the most appropriate
interpretation. Overall, this work provides a model system for quantitative
studies of influence and information in complex systems.

title: Robust Inference when Nuisance Parameters may be Partially Identified with Applications to Synthetic Controls
summary:
When conducting inference for the average treatment effect on the treated
with a Synthetic Control Estimator, the vector of control weights is a nuisance
parameter which is often constrained, high-dimensional, and may be only
partially identified even when the average treatment effect on the treated is
point-identified. All three of these features of a nuisance parameter can lead
to failure of asymptotic normality for the estimate of the parameter of
interest when using standard methods. I provide a new method yielding
asymptotic normality for an estimate of the parameter of interest, even when
all three of these complications are present. This is accomplished by first
estimating the nuisance parameter using a regularization penalty to achieve a
form of identification, and then estimating the parameter of interest using
moment conditions that have been orthogonalized with respect to the nuisance
parameter. I present high-level sufficient conditions for the estimator and
verify these conditions in an example involving Synthetic Controls.

title: The z=1.03 Merging Cluster SPT-CL J0356-5337: New Strong Lensing Analysis with HST and MUSE
summary:
We present a strong lensing analysis and reconstruct the mass distribution of
SPT-CL J0356-5337, a galaxy cluster at redshift z = 1.034. Our model supersedes
previous models by making use of new multi-band HST data and MUSE spectroscopy.
We identify two additional lensed galaxies to inform a more well-constrained
model using 12 sets of multiple images in 5 separate lensed sources. The three
previously-known sources were spectroscopically confirmed by Mahler et al.
(2020) at redshifts of z = 2.363, z = 2.364, and z = 3.048. We measured the
spectroscopic redshifts of two of the newly-discovered arcs using MUSE data, at
z = 3.0205 and z = 5.3288. We increase the number of cluster member galaxies by
a factor of three compared to previous work. We also report the detection of
extended Lya emission from several background galaxies. We measure the total
projected mass density of the two major sub-cluster components, one dominated
by the BCG, and the other by a compact group of luminous red galaxies. We find
M_BCG(< 80kpc) = 3.93+0.21-0.14 * 10^13Msun and M_LRG(< 80kpc) = 2.92+0.16
-0.23 * 10^13Msun, yielding a mass ratio of 1.35+0.16 -0.08. The strong lensing
constraints offer a robust estimate of the projected mass density regardless of
modelling assumptions; allowing more substructure in this line of sight does
not change the results or conclusions. Our results corroborate the conclusion
that SPT-CL J0356-5337 is dominated by two mass components, and is likely
undergoing a major merger on the plane of the sky

title: Quantitative U/Th deposition and cleanliness control strategies in the JUNO site air
summary:
The Jiangmen underground neutrino observatory (JUNO) is made of a 20 kt
liquid scintillator (LS) detector at a depth of 700 m underground. In order to
meet all physics requirements, the $^{238}$U/$^{232}$Th content in the LS is
required to reach a level of 10$^{-17}$ g/g. However, the radioactivity of dust
in the air is about 12 orders of magnitude higher than that, so there is an
extremely high requirement for the cleanliness of the installation environment
on site. In this study, a clean room management mode was implemented in the
120,000 m$^3$ space of the JUNO underground experimental main hall, to control
the environmental cleanliness at a level equivalent to a class 10,000-100,000
clean room. Additionally, we designed a method to directly measure the
deposition rate of $^{238}$U/$^{232}$Th on the surface of the detector. Based
on ICP-MS detection, the sensitivity to $^{238}$U/$^{232}$Th concentrations can
reach the level of picograms (pg). This helps to implement the cleanliness
control strategies and to assess the level of external contamination during the
construction of the detector.

title: Active Intracellular Mechanics: A Key to Cellular Function and Organization
summary:
While mechanobiology has demonstrated that precise control over mechanical
properties at the whole-cell level is crucial for many biological functions,
comparatively little attention has been paid to the intracellular mechanical
properties. Experimental tools have only recently become available to
adequately measure the viscoelasticity and activity of the cytosol, revealing,
revealing that the active, non-equilibrium nature of the intracellular
environment must be carefully considered.
  To explore the interplay between active forces and viscoelastic properties,
it is helpful to consider our current understanding of intracellular active
mechanics. In this review, we aim not only to provide an intuitive and
quantitative introduction to the relevant physical concepts, but also to offer
an overview of the proteins that establish intracellular active mechanics,
highlighting their spatial and temporal variation with a particular focus on
the role of activity.
  Although we are only beginning to uncover the importance of intracellular
active mechanics for cellular mechanisms, it is increasingly clear that these
properties must be precisely regulated to ensure proper cellular function.
